C arbonylation
Palladium-Catalyzed Carbonylative Multicomponent
Fluoroalkylation of 1,3-Enynes: Concise Construction of Diverse
Cyclic Compounds
Chang-Sheng Kuai, Bing-Hong Teng, and Xiao-Feng Wu*
Abstract: Multicomponent reactions, particularly those
entailing four or more reagents, have presented a
longstanding challenge due to the inherent complexities
associated with balancing reactivity, selectivity, and
compatibility. In this study, we describe a palladium-
catalyzed multi-component fluoroalkylative carbonyla-
tion of 1,3-enynes. A series of products featuring three
active functional groups-allene, fluoroalkyl, and
carboxyl, were efficiently and selectively integrated in a
single chemical operation. Furthermore, more intricate
fluoroalkyl-substituted pyrimidinones can be con-
structed by simply altering the 1,3-bisnucleophilic re-
agent. This approach also provides a valuable strategy
for the late-stage modification of naturally occurring
molecules and concise construction of diverse cyclic
compounds.
A llenes, serving as reactive intermediates, participate in a
diverse array of organic transformations and are ubiqui-
tously present in natural products, pharmaceuticals, and
functional materials (Scheme 1A).
[1]
Simultaneously, the
versatility of fluorine and fluoroalkyl moieties has been duly
acknowledged in the realm of functional groups. The
incorporation of these fluorine-laden motifs into the organic
framework invariably leads to the modification of the
physiological properties of the parent molecules, culminate
in heightened lipophilicity, increase bioavailability, and
improve metabolic stability.
[2]
Moreover, derivatives bearing
carboxylic acid functionality are prevalent in both pharma-
ceutical compounds and functional materials.
[3]
Considering
the pivotal roles that these three moieties play in the
domains of organic synthesis and medicinal chemistry, their
amalgamation within a singular molecular entity holds the
promise of substantial and transformative advantages for

endeavors such as drug discovery, pharmaceutical synthesis,
and the development of novel materials.
Multicomponent reactions (MCRs), possessing the
capability to forge numerous carbon-carbon or carbon-
heteroatom bonds from simple starting materials in one
synthetic operation, represent a compelling strategy in
organic synthesis owing to their capacity to enhance both
reaction efficiency and productivity.
[4]
In recent years,
transition metal-catalyzed carbonylation of unsaturated
bonds,
[3g,5]
the incorporation of carbon monoxide (a
pivotal bulk C1 building block) into organic molecular
frameworks through multicomponent reactions (MCRs)
have emerged as a potent strategy for accessing value-
added compounds, including pharmaceuticals and com-
moditized chemicals. Recently, innovative approaches
leveraging Pd-catalyzed domino perfluoroalkylation/car-
bonylation of olefins
[6]
and alkynes
[7]
have been devised
for the synthesis of β-perfluoroalkyl-substituted unsatu-
rated carbonyl-containing compounds. In contrast to
relatively straightforward substrates such as olefins and
alkynes with relatively singular selectivity (Scheme 1B),
the 1,3-enyne, characterized by the simultaneous pres-
ence of both alkene and alkyne functionalities, serves as
a common and valuable building block in synthetic
chemistry,
[8]
raising the difficulties associated with the in-
sequence control of the chemo-, regioselectivity. As
illustrated in Scheme 1B, a minimum of three distinct
regioselective structures is juxtaposed against the singu-
lar selectivity of either alkenes or alkynes.
Moreover, diverse chemoselectivity in a multicompo-
nent reaction can concomitantly generate undesired by-
products. Transition metal-catalyzed bisfunctionalization
of 1,3-enynes has undergone extensive investigation.
[8c,d,9]
While monofunctional carbonylation of 1,3-enynes has
been reported by Alper and Wu groups,
[10]
strategies
involving domino fluoroalkylation/carbonylation of the
more challenging 1,3-alkynes have remained elusive. As
the continuation of our research interests in catalytic
carbonylation chemistry, and considering the widespread
applicability and unique properties of the alkene, fluo-
roalkyl, and carboxyl groups, our interest has been
piqued by the potential of utilizing a multicomponent
transition metal-catalyzed domino fluoroalkylation/car-
bonylation reaction to achieve the one-step synthesis of
compounds incorporating all three of these functional
groups simultaneously. To date, a streamlined synthetic
method for construction of allene compounds containing
both carboxyl and fluoroalkyl functionalities has yet to
be replenished. Herein, we present an efficient palla-
dium-catalyzed, highly chemo- and regioselective multi-
component fluoroalkylative carbonylation of 1,3-enynes
for the synthesis of fluoroalkyl-substituted allene carbox-
ylic derivatives. Moreover, when employing 1,3-bisnu-
cleophilic substrates, further cyclization yields fluoroalk-

electron-withdrawing groups at the para-position of the
phenyl ring can also be applied, afforded the correspond-
ing products in 49–57 % yields (4 i–4 k). Due to the steric
hindrance inherent in this transformation, a notable
decrease in yield was observed when testing ortho-
substituted aniline derivatives (4 l, 4 m). Subsequently,
various ortho- and meta-substituted anilines were sub-
jected for further testing. Anilines with different func-
tional groups, including bromo-, trifluoromethyl-, amide-
, nitrile-, and even hydroxy-, were well tolerated,
afforded the corresponding products 4 n–4 t in moderate
yields. Nevertheless, heterocyclic substituted amines,
such as thiophene and pyridine, impede the reaction and
delivers the target products in moderate yields (4 x, 4 y).
However, no desired product could be detected when N-
methylaniline, alkyl amines or benzamide were tested as
the reaction partners which most likely due to the not
matched basicity.
Subsequently, with alcohols as the nucleophile, a
series of fluoroalkyl-substituted allene esters were syn-
thesized in moderate yields (5 a–5 i). For instance, sub-
strates containing functional groups such as methoxy,
iodide, and olefins exhibit compatibility with this proc-
ess. Moreover, potentially attributed to the phenol’s
capacity to quench free radicals, the attainment of the
target product was limited to 27 % yield. In addition to
the primary alcohols, secondary alcohols are also toler-
ated and deliver the corresponding products (5 h, 5 i).
However, tertiary alcohol, characterized by high steric
hindrance, yield only trace amounts of product 5 j.

phenylpropyl) and diverse heteroatom-substituted alkyl
groups (OBz, OTBS and OAc) on the R
1
-position of 1,3-

the impact of varying R

When R
2
was altered to phenyl or ethyl, the correspond-

yields, respectively. However, the yield of the diphenyl-
substituted 1,3-enyne (6 u) decreased to 40 %. When R
2

observed (6 v, 6 w). This distinct reactivity may arise from
the instability of the formed propargyl radical and the
derived allenyl radical.
Finally, a variety of fluoroalkyl halides, including
diverse polyfluorinated long-chain alkyl iodide or bro-
mine substrates, bromodifluoroacetate, and ethyl 2-
bromo-2-fluoroacetate, underwent smooth reactions,
yielding the corresponding products 7 a–7 e in moderate
yields. Additionally, it was noteworthy to discover that
perfluoroiodopropane (7 f, 7 g) could also participate in
the reaction and afforded 57 % to 63 % yields of the
corresponding products. However, no desired product
was detected when 1-fluoro-3-iodopropane was tested as
the substrate.
Given that allenes are a highly reactive class of
substrates, we envisaged the possibility of employing
bisnucleophilic substrates for subsequent reactions with
allenes after the fluoroalkylative carbonylation of 1,3-
enynes, aiming to obtain more complex products. Ini-
tially, we employed bisnucleophilic substrates such as
guanidine, urea, thiourea and diol, but none of them
exhibited reactivity. We speculate that this might be
attributed to the hindrance of the initial step of
fluoroalkylative carbonylation of 1,3-enynes. Subse-
quently, we turn to potentially bisnucleophilic hetero-
cyclic aromatic amine substrates (Scheme 4). To our
delight, when oxazol-2-amine was employed, further
cyclization of the product pyrimidinone (8 a) could be
obtained in 70 % yield without further optimization the
reaction conditions. Other heterocyclic amines, such as
thiazol-2-amine, oxazol-2-amine and N-methyl-benzoimi-
dazol-2-amine, were all well compatible in the reaction
(8 b, 8 e and 8 f). However, saturated 4,5-dihydrothiazol-
2-amine and 1H-imidazol-2-amine exhibit no reactivity
(8 c, 8 d), and we speculate that this may be attributed to
their strong alkalinity, causing the reaction to stagnate.
Afterwards, we shifted our focus to the compatibility of
1,3-alkyne derivatives in this conversion. Various aryl-
substituted 2-methyl-1, 3-enes are involved in this reac-
tion without any problem. Both substrates containing
electron-donating groups and electron-withdrawing
groups in the phenyl ring were all tolerated, and the
yields of corresponding products is between 52 % and
76 % (8 g–8 k). However, when the alkyl-substituted 1, 3-
alkyne was employed in the reaction, the alkene isomer-
ization product 8 l was obtained in 21 %.
To further illustrate the synthetic utility of this
strategy, several experiments were conducted as depicted
in Scheme 5. Initially, various natural products and
bioactive molecule modified amines and alcohols were
investigated to verify the practicability of this method.
Gratifyingly, biologically active and naturally occurring
amines, such as DL-menthol (4 z), dimethocaine (4 aa),
amino acid derivatives (4 ab, 4 ad), coumarin 120 (4 ac)
aminoglutethimide (4 ae), Vitamin E (4 af), and mosapr-
ide (4 ag), were all successfully converted into the
corresponding products in 49 %–83 % yields (Sche-
me 5A). Furthermore, bioactive alcohols such as dehy-
droepiandrosterone (5 k) and cholesterol (5 l) showed
low reactivity, afforded the corresponding products in
48 % and 36 % yields, respectively. The successful
applications of this method to these complex molecules
will have significant implications for the discovery and
research of drugs and materials. Next, two scale-up
transformations with aniline and ethanol gave acceptable
yields (4 a, 61 %; 5 a, 58 %), respectively (Scheme 5B).
The fluoroalkyl substituted allene carboxylic derivatives,
as useful synthetic intermediates, can be converted to
other versatile chemicals. Thus, concise and divergent
constructions of various cyclic compounds have been
demonstrated, as shown in Scheme 5C.

phile (1 f) exhibit faster nucleophilic capabilities com-
pared to electron-deficient substrate (1 i). When different

Based on our mechanistic studies and related
literatures,
[9e,i,13]
a palladium-mediated radical mechanism
is proposed (Scheme 7). The catalytic cycle initiates with
the formation of the active catalyst Pd
0
Ln species A,
generated in situ from the Pd(COD)Cl
2
. Then, complex
A induced a single-electron transfer (SET) reduction of
Rf-X, leading to the generation of the fluoroalkyl radical
B and Pd
I
LnX species E. Subsequently, the fluoroalkyl
radical B was captured by enyne 2 to yield a tertiary
propargyl radical C, which can be isomerized to rela-
tively stable allenyl radical D. Following this, the Pd
I
LnX
species E reincorporated with the allenyl radical D to
afford the Pd
II

carbon monoxide to provide intermediate G. Finally,
intermediate G reacts with nucleophile 1 to produce the
desired fluoroalkylative carbonylation products (4 or 5)
and regenerate Pd
0
Ln for the next catalytic cycle with the
assistance of base. Notably, when employed bisnucleo-
phile 1’ reacts with intermediate G to afford intermediate
H, which underwent nucleophilic addition with allene to
give the cyclization products 8.
In conclusion, we have developed an efficient palla-
dium-catalyzed multi-component fluoroalkylative car-
bonylation of 1,3-enynes. A broad range of fluoroalkyl
substituted allene carboxylic derivatives were prepared
successfully with high chemo- and regio- selectivities and
outstanding functional group tolerance. Additionally,
more intricate fluoroalkyl-substituted pyrimidinones can
be constructed by simply altering the 1,3-bisnucleophilic
reagent. This approach also provides a valuable strategy
for the late-stage modification of naturally occurring
molecules and concisely constructing diverse cyclic com-
pounds.
